HEADLINE: Firms tackle the scourge of slavery
TEXT:
Retail behemoth Wesfarmers has ended contracts with 20 suppliers over concerns about modern slavery, with instances of worker exploitation across its supply chain more than doubling last year.

An initial wave of 121 statements by Australian and overseas companies, including many household names, has been published on an Australian Border Force register as part of new government requirements under the Modern Slavery Act.

Modern slavery encompasses a range of serious practices such as human trafficking, slavery, forced labour and debt bondage. Estimates suggest there are 1900 victims of modern slavery in Australia at any one time and 16 million globally.

Under the Modern Slavery Act, companies based or operating in Australia with annual revenue greater than $100 million are required to prepare annual statements outlining actions they are taking to assess and prevent modern slavery risks in their operations.

Wesfarmers, whose brands include Bunnings, Kmart and Officeworks, said it identified 340 critical breaches across 105 suppliers in 2019-20, up from 127 breaches a year earlier.

"The majority of critical breaches included allegations of excessive overtime, transparency (record keeping and documentation), safety (building and fire safety), unauthorised subcontracting and bribery," the company's report said.

Three suppliers had their contracts terminated immediately over four serious breaches, while no further orders were placed with 17 suppliers over 40 breaches.

However, 161 breaches were remedied promptly and 135 on track to do so.

Audits conducted by Woolworths across its supply chain identified seafood, cocoa and nuts as the top three food products most vulnerable to modern slavery issues, while for non-food products it was cotton, furniture and garments.

Responding to concerns about forced labour in the Chinese province of Xinjiang, Woolworths said it was tracing its garment supply chain in the region.

Assistant Customs Minister Jason Wood said the publication of the statements provided consumers, businesses, investors, civil society and regulators with an unprecedented window into the operations and global supply chains of major Australian businesses.

"There is no excuse for inaction on this issue and every business should be taking steps to ensure they understand modern slavery risks in their operations and supply chains, and implementing measures to address them," he said.

HEADLINE: COVIDSafe app to be given major overhaul
TEXT:
The Morrison government's COVIDSafe app is to be overhauled to capture 100 per cent of close contacts of infected people who have the app.

The expected large improvement in detecting close contacts comes as the federal government is preparing a new pre-Christmas campaign to promote good infection hygiene behaviours.

This follows concerns that Australia's near elimination of the coronavirus could result in an outbreak of unsafe behaviour that has driven large surges in infection in the US and Europe.

Health Minister Greg Hunt wants the campaign to be a reminder about community complacency, as Apple mobility data show a return to above normal driving activity.

Mid-year the app's Bluetooth protocol was reporting poor (less than 25 per cent of contacts) to good (50 to 80 per cent of contacts) performance across various conditions, with the best performance being achieved only when the app was active and the phone unlocked.

The overhaul will incorporate a new Bluetooth protocol called Herald that promises 100 per cent app-level Bluetooth performance to better identify potential close contacts. The update is expected to lead to improvements in contact tracing, integrated with state and territory health authorities' contact tracing systems.

A report by Chief Scientist Alan Finkel endorsed research that showed contacts must be isolated within 48 hours of testing to best stop the spread of infection. The national cabinet has now endorsed this as a key performance measure and is now being reported on publicly as part of the common operating picture.

The COVIDSafe app logs "close contacts" - people who also have the app and are within 1.5 metres of each other for 15 minutes over a 14-day period. If a person with the app becomes infectious the detected close contacts can be directly downloaded by the local public health teams. .

New code is to be released on the open-source site Github for community review this week, ahead of proposed incorporation into the app stores of Google and Apple.

Testing by the Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) on behalf of the federal health department has shown 100 per cent performance, scoring "excellent" in all operating modes.

The DTA has been working with Apple and Google on incorporating the new protocol in the COVIDSafe app and has performed extensive testing across Android and iOS devices.

Government Services Minister Stuart Robert is expected to release the code for public review by infosecurity and privacy experts today. If acceptable, authorities are planning to release the new Herald code base for global use by the wide variety of Bluetooth tracing apps now available.

According to DTA tests the new protocol will continue to work on more than 96 per cent of Apple and Android phones. The only scenario where the app will not capture all "close contacts" is when the app is not active.

According to federal officials the COVIDSafe App has assisted in identifying close contacts not picked up through manual tracing in New South Wales and Victoria. In NSW the COVIDSafe app has identified 80 close contacts, including 17 contacts that were not identified by manually contact tracing.

In one instance, the COVIDSafe app revealed a previously unrecognised exposure date from a known venue called the Mounties. This resulted in the identification of an additional 544 contacts, with two people subsequently confirmed to have COVID-19.

Victoria stopped using the COVIDSafe app at the height of the second wave in August as it had not been integrated into their contact tracing process.

At that time only 50 per cent of people tested positive were being told within 24 hours, leading to the contact tracing system being overwhelmed, according to local officials.

HEADLINE: Growing cyber risk an opportunity
TEXT:
The increasing threat posed by cyber criminals and state-based hackers represents a major opportunity for Australia to develop a thriving export market for security products and services, a new report finds.

While the downside risk of cyber insecurity is well established, the report's authors say the focus should be on the upside opportunities from the $147 billion-a-year global market in cyber security products and services.

AustCyber's industry competitiveness plan 2020 update reveals the domestic cyber security market will generate $3.6 billion in revenue this year - a 20 per cent increase from 2017 - and has a gross value add to the Australian economy of $2.3 billion a year.

That figure is expected to more than double to $7.6 billion by 2024 and add about 7000 new jobs, bringing the total cyber security workforce to 33,500 positions.

But high barriers of entry, access to skills and financing to develop products and ideas, an underdeveloped export presence overseas, and a rapidly dwindling skills pipeline are putting that opportunity at risk.

AustCyber chief executive Michelle Price told The Australian Financial Review that Australa's cyber security sector was coming into its own, with more than 350 sovereign providers employing more than 26,500 workers.

"The growth in the number of companies producing globally competitive products and services has, comparative to other industries, exploded."

The sector was also well positioned to take advantage of the uptake of digital technologies in the COVID-19 economic recovery, she said, but could not be complacent.

"While we are well placed for further growth and success as the sector continues to tackle familiar challenges relating to innovation, market maturity, investment and skills, more needs to be done to ramp up the momentum over the next 12 months, and slowing down is not an option."

More than 40 per cent of Australian cyber security companies are already exporting into overseas markets, reflecting that the domestic market "is not large enough to sustain companies that can compete with global cyber security providers".

But exports account for only 15 per cent of the sector's revenue.

The report calls on government to engage more directly with local cyber security suppliers, expand Australia's export presence in the US, UK and key Asian markets, boost support for domestic cyber security research hubs, make it easier to overcome market barriers, and maintain a skills pipeline.

"New providers with quality offerings need to be supported, funded, connected to the market, and supplied with the skilled workers they need to succeed," the report said. "Governments, cyber security leaders, educators and investors all have crucial roles to play as the sector matures."

The report showed large diversified technology companies that integrate systems and security are receiving the largest share of revenue ($1.5 billion), followed by SMEs ($800 million), major consultancies and mid-tier firms ($500 million each), and defence specific providers ($300 million).

Most cyber security firms are small businesses with between five and 20 employees (40 per cent), followed by micro firms with fewer than five employees (25 per cent), and firms with up to 100 employees (25 per cent).

AustCyber's Australia's Digital Trust Report 2020 says a major cyber offensive would be far more disruptive than the coronavirus pandemic.

HEADLINE: Star duo behind Macquarie's greatest hit with $1.8b Nuix float
TEXT:
The $1.8 billion float of intelligence software giant Nuix on Friday is a big moment on many levels but for Macquarie's Dan Phillips and David Standen it looms as one of the biggest of their careers.

The tech sector will add another publicly listed giant to its ranks and the ASX another robust and truly global member for its All Technology Index.

It is a big moment for Nuix staff, who are set to share in a bonanza of stock and options.

And it's a big moment for early Nuix investors, such as Melbourne power couple Alan and Carol Schwartz. The growth capital firm they control, Armitage Associates, will sell about $48 million of shares in the float, and retain a stake worth the same amount.

Phillips and Standen, who head Macquarie Group's venture capital team, bought into Nuix in 2011, with reports putting the group's total investment over a couple of tranches between $100 million and $150 million.

Based on Nuix's offer price of $5.31 a share, Macquarie will reap about $566 million in the float and retain a 30 per cent stake in the business worth $508 million.

No wonder the IPO is already being talked up as one of the most profitable deals in Macquarie's history, even bigger than the windfalls the Silver Doughnut famously enjoyed in the float of explosives maker Dyno Nobel in 2006, or from the IPO of mining services group Boart Longyear a year later.

But Nuix is far from Phillips' and Standen's only success. Over 25 years, the duo has invested about $700 million in 36 ventures across a myriad of sectors with what Phillips says is a 90 per cent strike rate.

In addition to the $1 billion return they will deliver Macquarie through the Nuix IPO, Phillips and Standen also steered property software group PEXA to a $1.6 billion trade sale and a $400 million return in 2018, and took about $155 million off the table in 2016 when they helped float Dutch online ordering platform Takeaway.com.

Remarkably, this has all been done well below the radar; Phillips and Standen are not even that well known in Australia's tight-knit venture capital community, where successes are usually celebrated loudly.

James Thomson back page

HEADLINE: UK to approve Pfizer vaccine 'within days'
TEXT:
Britain is poised to become the first Western country to approve a COVID-19 vaccine, with the independent regulator set to grant approval within days.

Deliveries of the vaccine, developed by BioNTech and Pfizer, would begin within hours of the authorisation and the first injections could take place from December 7. Britain has ordered 40 million doses, which preliminary data found to be more than 95 per cent effective in preventing disease.

HEADLINE: Speedier recovery drops demand for JobKeeper
TEXT:
The JobKeeper wage subsidy is being paid to 700,000 fewer people than forecast in the October 6 budget, which the federal government says shows the economy is recovering faster than anticipated.

The latest Australian Taxation Office data released by Treasurer Josh Frydenberg yesterday shows the number of JobKeeper recipients fell from 3.6 million employees working for almost 1 million businesses under the old scheme, which ran from March to September, to 1.5 million working for about 500,000 businesses, under the new, two-tiered scheme.

These 1.5 million employees are far fewer than the 2.2 million employees who were forecast in the budget to need the new subsidy, signalling that their employers no longer meet the decline in turnover to qualify.

"The lower-than-forecast take-up of the JobKeeper payment extension in October is further evidence that Australia's recovery from this once-in-a-century pandemic is well under way," Mr Frydenberg said.

The upbeat numbers have been released ahead of Wednesday's economic growth figures for the September quarter, which will show Australia's run of two successive quarters of contraction have come to an end and the economy is no longer in recession.

Despite the shutdown of the Victorian economy over successive months which added $15 billion to the cost of JobKeeper and wiped more than $10 billion from national GDP, the September quarter is expected to bounce back strongly, even if coming off a low base. The economy contracted a massive 7 per cent in the June quarter.

The big four banks all expect 3 per cent to 4.1 per cent growth in the September quarter, which would be the highest since 1976.

If realised, this would also fuel upward revisions to growth forecasts in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook (MYEFO) to be released in mid-December. The government will wait until the GDP numbers on Wednesday before finalising MYEFO.

The recovery is being fuelled by stronger retail spending, continued job hiring, higher house prices, record consecutive consumer confidence readings, news of an early vaccine and almost $500 billion in government and central bank stimulus pumping into the economy as COVID-19 restrictions are relaxed.

Consistent with the optimism of a speedy recovery, banks are also reporting loan deferrals to be falling faster than anticipated and homeowners and SMEs find themselves able to resume payments.

The first tranche of JobKeeper, which ran over 13 fortnights from March to September 27, paid a flat, $1500 payment to 3.6 million workers from 1 million businesses, at a cost to the federal budget of about $70 billion.

To qualify for the first tranche, a business with less than $1 billion turnover had to show a 30 per cent decline compared to the March quarter last year. Those with turnovers over $1 billion had to show a 50 per cent decline.

To qualify for JobKeeper 2.0, a business with an annual turnover of less than $1 billion must show its turnover has fallen more than 30 per cent between this September quarter and the same quarter last year.

The $1500 flat subsidy was replaced with a $750 subsidy for those who worked fewer than 20 hours a week before the crisis struck, and $1200 for all others.

Of the 1.5 million current recipients, 86 per cent, or about 1.3 million, are on the higher subsidy and the remainder on the lower subsidy.

Mr Frydenberg suggested had it not been for Victoria's collapse, the recovery would be in even better shape.

The 1.5 million employees on the new JobKeeper arrangement are close to the 1.4 million employees Treasury originally forecast would qualify on July 31, when the new scheme was announced.

At the time, Victoria had not entered the stage four lockdown.
